name: Punch excision / punch elevation

lead: Punch excision and punch elevation are minor surgical techniques for atrophic acne scars, particularly deep boxcar scars with sharp edges. The payoff is smoother-looking cheeks where deep pits are removed or raised level with the surrounding skin.

In punch excision, a small circular blade removes the scar and the wound is closed; in punch elevation, the scar base is cut free and raised level with the skin. Both were named in a widely cited 2001 review proposing the icepick, rolling and boxcar scar classification. Randomised trials identifying a best method are limited, and a 2024 review notes combining treatments would likely produce more benefit than a single method.

paras: A clinician performs the procedure under local anaesthetic, often scar by scar. It is usually followed by resurfacing such as lasers or dermabrasion to blend the treated area, with healing over days to weeks.

As surgical procedures they carry the general risks of skin surgery, including a residual or new scar, infection and pigment change. Reviews describe them as clinician-performed and as part of combined approaches.

chain: Deep scar cut out or lifted
angle.text: Punch excision and elevation are used on deep boxcar acne scars, either removing the scar or raising its base to skin level for a smoother-looking surface. The techniques are long established in dermatology, with limited trial-level data.

lead: Punch excision and punch elevation are minor surgical techniques used on atrophic acne scars, particularly deep boxcar scars with sharp edges, to make the skin surface of the face smoother and more even. In punch excision, a circular punch instrument removes the scar tissue and the defect is closed; in punch elevation, the base of the scar is separated and raised to the level of the surrounding skin [1][2]. People seeking clearer-looking skin use them to turn a visible pit into a flat line or a level surface.

Both were named in a widely cited 2001 review that proposed the icepick, rolling and boxcar classification of acne scars together with a treatment algorithm that also included subcision and laser resurfacing [1]. A 2006 Swiss review likewise lists punch excision, punch elevation, subcision, dermal graft and fat transplantation as the surgical options, with dermabrasion or laser resurfacing as complements [2].

A 2024 narrative review notes that few randomised controlled trials have been designed to determine a gold-standard treatment for acne scars and that combining interventions would likely produce more benefit than a single method [3]. In practice the punch techniques are usually one step in a multi-stage plan.

Scars are common after acne: Wikipedia estimates they affect about 95 percent of people with acne vulgaris, arising from dermal inflammation and abnormal healing, with atrophic (depressed) types making up roughly three quarters of them [4]. Punch techniques address the discrete, sharp-bordered pits among these, which is why dermatologists often use them on individual scars while treating the surrounding skin with other methods [1][2].
infobox: Deep boxcar and some icepick atrophic scars

paras: Atrophic acne scars are commonly divided into icepick (narrow, deep), boxcar (round or oval with sharp borders) and rolling (broad, wave-like) types [1][4]. According to Wikipedia, atrophic scars make up about 75 percent of acne scars and boxcar scars are roughly 1.5 to 4 mm across [4]. Treatment is generally matched to scar type, and punch techniques are associated in the literature with discrete, well-defined depressions rather than broad rolling scars [1][2].

Punch excision removes the scar and relies on closure to leave a finer line. Punch elevation raises the scar base so it sits level with the neighbouring skin, and reviews describe resurfacing as a frequent follow-up to smooth remaining differences [1][2]. The article does not describe step-by-step technique.

Wikipedia gives approximate sizes for the scar types: icepick scars are narrow, under 2 mm, and extend deep into the dermis; boxcar scars are about 1.5 to 4 mm across; rolling scars are broader, around 4 to 5 mm, with a wave-like pattern [4]. Because the punch is a round instrument sized to the lesion, the approach suits boxcar and some icepick scars whose edges are well defined, while rolling scars are generally treated with methods that release tethering beneath the skin, such as subcision [1][4]. Punch grafting, a related technique, fills the defect with a small piece of skin rather than closing it directly [1].

A 2019 Dermatologic Surgery update using the same classification lists surgical modalities, including subcision and punch excision and elevation, alongside injectable fillers, chemical peels, dermabrasion, microneedling and energy-based devices, and observes a trend in the past decade toward fillers and energy-based devices; it also concludes that few high-quality studies evaluate acne scar management [5]. A 2011 Aesthetic Plastic Surgery review of acne scarring in the aging face similarly describes a multimodal approach, with resurfacing for surface irregularities, fillers for volume loss, and subcision or punch excision for individual scars, illustrated by case examples [6]. A 2020 review of post-acne scarring in skin of color graded the level of evidence for each modality by scar type and noted that guidelines specific to skin of color are not available [7]. A 2024 JAAD article on procedural and surgical treatments for acne scarring is another overview [8].

The modern framework for choosing among scar treatments comes from a 2001 review in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology, which classified atrophic scars as icepick, boxcar or rolling and proposed matching each to a treatment, including punch excision and elevation for discrete pits [1]. That classification is still used by later reviews, including a 2019 update in Dermatologic Surgery that reassessed treatment options as fillers and energy-based devices became more common [5]. A 2006 Swiss review of the surgical role in acne scars grouped punch excision, punch elevation, subcision, dermal graft and fat transplantation as the surgical options [2].

Punch work is rarely the only step. Wikipedia describes subcision, in which a small needle releases fibrotic bands that tether superficial atrophic scars; fillers such as hyaluronic acid or autologous fat that add volume and reduce depth; microneedling, used especially in darker skin, whose side effects include post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and tram-track scarring when technique is poor; chemical peels ranging from superficial acids to deep trichloroacetic acid; dermabrasion, now less used since lasers arrived; and nonablative and ablative laser resurfacing, with the ablative types carrying higher rates of pigment change, persistent redness and pain [4].

A 2011 review on aging faces describes combining resurfacing, fillers and subcision or punch excision for different parts of the same scarring pattern [6], and the 2020 review on skin of color grades modalities by scar type and notes the lack of dedicated guidelines [7]. Wikipedia notes that pigmentation after skin injury is more common in darker skin and can last months or years, which is a consideration when choosing among these methods [4].

No randomised trial dedicated to punch excision or punch elevation alone for acne scars was identified. The techniques are described within treatment-algorithm and narrative reviews [1][3][2], and the 2024 review states that randomised data to rank acne scar treatments are limited [3]. The 2001 review's algorithm combined punch techniques with subcision and laser resurfacing rather than testing them in isolation [1].

Punch excision has been studied in combination in related contexts. A 2011 pilot study evaluated punch excision combined with erbium:YAG fractional laser on different scar types in Asian patients [9]. For keloids, a 2023 randomized controlled trial of 81 patients tested punch excision combined with intralesional steroid injection [10], a 2026 single-blinded randomized trial compared punch excision plus triamcinolone and 5-fluorouracil injection with a manual fractional technology approach [11], and a 2025 systematic review examined punch excision therapy in keloids [12]. These concern raised scars rather than acne pits.

Quantified complication rates for these specific techniques have not been reported. As procedures that cut the skin, they involve general surgical considerations such as healing, possible residual scarring and pigment change, and reviews place them with clinicians rather than home use [3][2]. Wikipedia notes that post-inflammatory pigmentation after skin injury can last months or years, particularly with sun exposure [4].

Wikipedia's discussion of pigmentation after skin injury says it can be sustained by sun exposure, which is why sun protection is commonly advised during healing [4]. Other procedures often paired with punch work have their own risk profiles, such as the higher adverse-effect rates of ablative lasers [4].

The procedure is categorised on the wiki under hardmaxx, the community's label for invasive appearance interventions, because of its role in treating deep scars. Skin quality, including acne scars, appears on looksmax.org in lists of facial problems users hope to improve, though threads mentioning punch techniques specifically are not cited here [13].

A review of surgical options for acne scars lists punch excision and elevation alongside subcision and grafting [2].

A review describes multimodal management of atrophic acne scarring with punch excision for individual scars, and a pilot study combines punch excision with fractional erbium:YAG laser in Asian patients [6][9].
A Dermatologic Surgery update to the scar classification system observes a shift toward fillers and energy-based devices and few high-quality studies [5].
